On 22 July 2026 at 15:05, I made the first commit to a new repository. It held an empty R package and one Excel workbook of 3.4 MB with field data from a household waste study in Kampala, Uganda. Three minutes later I sent the first prompt to Claude Code:

> I am building a new data package and received a dataset in @data-raw/ to
> process for clean up. […] strictly start with cleaning the data, writing a
> dictionary. […] make a plan first.

On 24 July at 00:18, the same repository held version 1.0.0 of [solidwastekampala](https://github.com/openwashdata/solidwastekampala) with a Zenodo DOI. It contains a tidy and validated dataset of 103 households, a data dictionary for 37 variables, documentation, a website, machine-readable metadata, a citation with the ORCID iDs of the authors, and automated checks on five platforms.

That was 33 hours on the calendar and about nine hours of work in four sessions. The repository keeps a record of every step in its commits, issues and pull requests, and in an archive of every prompt I sent. This post retells the story from that record.

## The data

The dataset belongs to the paper [Quantity and composition of domestic solid waste in Kampala City as influenced by socioeconomic factors](https://doi.org/10.3389/fenvs.2026.1889921) by Katukiza et al. at Makerere University, published in Frontiers in Environmental Science in September 2026. Field teams weighed and sorted the waste of 103 households over seven days in three parishes that stand for three income levels. Bwaise I is the low income parish, Bukoto I the middle income parish and Ggaba the high income parish. Each record combines the mass of ten waste categories, values derived per household, and the socioeconomic characteristics of the household.

The data arrived the way field data usually arrives. The workbook had several sheets with two rows of merged headers, summary rows at the bottom, sheets with derived results next to the raw ones, and the typos that manual data entry leaves behind.

## Session 1: a plan before any code

The first session produced no cleaning code at all. It produced a plan, and writing the plan required a close look at every sheet of the workbook. That look settled several questions before anything was changed.

- Only three sheets hold raw data. The sheet called "All_data" consolidates them and stays in the package as a cross-check. All other sheets hold derived results.
- The 103 households split into 39, 32 and 32 across the three parishes, as in the paper.
- Exactly one number in the workbook is stored as text. A cell for metals in Ggaba reads `2..674`, and the SUM formula in Excel skipped it without a warning. The recorded totals therefore had to stay as they are, because the values per day, per person and the density are all calculated from them.
- The means per parish reproduce the headline figures of the paper, 0.43, 0.53 and 0.98 kg of waste per person per day. This confirmed that these were the right sheets to work from.

The plan also set the rule for the rest of the project. We preserve the data as recorded and do not polish it. Seven inconsistencies inside the workbook are documented and tested for, and none of them was corrected without a record.

## Session 2: from plan to package

Early on Wednesday the plan became GitHub issues, one per step and each small enough to review on its own. I asked for one issue at a time, with a stop for my review before each commit, and for the list of typos to be shown to me before anything was changed. One of the prompts that morning reads, in full, "now?".

By 06:55 the processing script was in place. It reads all three sheets as text so that nothing is lost on import, gives the 37 columns consistent names, fixes the `2..674` cell and repairs two malformed household IDs. A map per column harmonises the categories, for example `IIIiterate` to `Illiterate`, `Unpaced` to `Unpaved` and `Kawenpe Division` to `Kawempe`, and it merges seven spellings of the same income band into one. Five ordered categories became ordered factors. A validation block at the end of the script checks the result: 103 rows, no missing values and the right number of households per parish. It also checks the inconsistencies we know about. The sums of the waste categories match the recorded totals in 99 of 103 rows, and the script names the four exceptions.

At 07:19 I merged the first pull request with the clean data, CSV and XLSX exports, and a dictionary that describes all 37 variables with units and categories. At 08:03 the second pull request followed with what a stranger needs to use the data: the package metadata, documentation generated from the dictionary, a README with an example that reproduces a figure of the paper, a website, and metadata in schema.org format.

## Session 3: the review

Every openwashdata package goes through a review against a versioned standard. This package used version 1.0.0 of that standard, and the version is recorded in the repository so that anyone can see which standard was applied. The review consists of four checklist issues, and each one closes with its own pull request.

| Step | Issue | Pull request | Merged |
|---|---|---|---|
| Metadata and citation | #14 | #16 | 12:22 |
| Data content and processing | #17 | #18 | 12:58 |
| Documentation | #19 | #20 | 13:52 |
| Tests and automated checks | #21 | #22 | 14:50 |

The metadata step looked up the ORCID iDs of the co-authors in the public registry and found five. Two of the matches were uncertain, so the step opened issue #15 and asked the main author to confirm them. It also noticed that one record spelled a given name "Abubakar" while the package said "Abubakkar". The data step ran the whole processing script again and confirmed that the result was identical, byte for byte, to the committed data. The documentation step extended the README. The last step added checks that install the package on five platforms and run its examples, with 0 errors, 0 warnings and 0 notes.

At 14:54 the review was complete.

## Session 4: the authors reply

The last missing piece came from the authors that evening. At 23:55 the prompt archive records my message "ORCIDs have arrived". The main author had confirmed the uncertain matches, sent the ORCID iD of Shaluwa Namagembe and settled the spelling as Abubakar, as in his own ORCID record. The corrections went into all metadata files and the website, and the author order now follows the paper. At 00:15 I released version 1.0.0, and at 00:18 Zenodo archived it and issued the DOI.

## How the package meets the FAIR principles

The package is findable through a DOI, [10.5281/zenodo.21519796](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21519796), which always resolves to the latest version, through its own [website](https://openwashdata.github.io/solidwastekampala/), and through schema.org metadata that search engines and data catalogues can read.

It is accessible in several formats for different users. R users install the package from GitHub, everyone else downloads CSV or XLSX files, and the Zenodo archive keeps a copy that does not depend on GitHub. The raw workbook stays in the package as well.

It is interoperable because the data are tidy, the names follow one convention, ordered categories are stored as ordered factors, and the files use UTF-8. The dataset has no missing values.

It is reusable because the dictionary describes all 37 variables with units, the processing script reproduces the data and doubles as a statement of data quality, the inconsistencies of the source are documented, and the data carry a CC BY 4.0 licence. At the release, seven of the eight authors had an ORCID iD checked against the public registry. The main author sent the iD of Alex Y. Katukiza on 28 July, and version 1.0.1 of 17 September carries all eight.

There is one more layer that the FAIR principles do not name, and that is the record of how the package was made. The repository archives every prompt in `prompts/`, with a timestamp and the files it touched, and every plan in `plans/`. Commit messages link to the prompts behind them. Anyone can trace how each decision was made, including the decision to keep the four inconsistent sums exactly as the field teams recorded them.

## What I take from it

Cleaning the data took about one hour of the nine. The rest went into the plan, the dictionary, the documentation, the metadata, the review, the citation, the exchange with the authors and the archive. That work is what turns a spreadsheet into a publication, and it is the reason why so many datasets never leave the hard drive. With the tools we have built over the years (washr, dataspice, pkgdown, GitHub Actions and Zenodo), a versioned review standard and an AI assistant that works through checklists, this work now fits into one afternoon and the following day.

## How I used AI

I used AI for this package and for this post, and the record of that use is public.

**The package.** Claude Code (model Claude Fable 5) wrote the processing script, the dictionary, the documentation and the metadata, following my prompts. The repository archives the 11 prompts I sent up to the release in `prompts/`, and 14 of the 39 commits made by 24 July carry an `Assisted-by` line that names the model. I asked for a plan before any code, for one issue at a time with a stop for my review, and for the list of typos before any change, and I added the harmonisations to that list. I reviewed and merged each of the eight pull requests, handled the exchange with the authors and settled the spelling of their names. The data do not depend on the AI. The processing script is plain R code, and anyone can rerun it without any AI tool and get the same data.

**This post.** Claude (model Claude Fable 5) wrote the first draft on 24 July in a session on the package repository, from the commits, issues, pull requests and prompts. On 7 October Claude (model Claude Opus 5.5) revised it at my request. It checked the text against my style rules, updated the facts that had changed since July (the published paper, the DOI for all versions, the eighth ORCID iD) and rewrote the text in my voice. <!-- Lars: confirm this sentence is true before publishing -->
I chose what the post says, checked every date and number against the repository, and decided to publish it.

I write AI use statements like this one because I think disclosure works best when it comes out of the record of the work, which is the position I take in my work on AI disclosure in research. The prompts, the commits and this post are in public repositories, so anyone can check the statement against the record.
